deep.reconstruction: No mathematics appears on this page. Folio 96v shows only the recto (96r) bleeding through the paper. The text is mirror-reversed, faint and brownish. It is the same English quotation from Newton's letter to Richard Bentley that is transcribed as the previous page: 'That gravity should be innate, inherent, and essential to matter, so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum, without the mediation of anything else, by and through which their action and force may be conveyed from one to another, is to me so great an absurdity, that I believe no man who has in philosophical matters a competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it.' Riemann's source note reads 'See the third letter to Bentley.' This matches Newton's letter of 25 February 1692/3, usually numbered the third of the Bentley letters. In the bundle this quotation sits beside Riemann's German notes on causality on the next page: an agent's action must be determined by its own concept; agents must be states or relations rather than things, which strive to maintain or restore themselves. In Riemann's natural philosophy the quotation supports his rejection of unmediated action at a distance. That rejection motivates his ether or medium-based theories of gravitation and light. There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.
The reference 'third letter to Bentley' is consistent with the standard numbering (letter of 25 Feb 1692/3), so it is not an error.

results.what: Quotation of Newton's rejection of unmediated action at a distance, used as a premise for a contact- or medium-based natural philosophy.
results.modern_name: Newton's letter to Bentley on action at a distance (philosophical motivation for field and ether theories)
results.usually_credited_to: Isaac Newton (1692/3); the quotation was widely used in the 19th century by Faraday, Maxwell and others.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is only show-through of a copied, well-known Newton quotation. Riemann's opposition to action at a distance and his medium-based theories of gravitation and light are well documented in his published natural-philosophy fragments. I am not certain whether this exact quotation appears in the editions of those fragments, but its presence would be unremarkable either way.
transcription_corrections: The visible writing on 96v is a mirror-image bleed-through of 96r, not text written on this side. The page should be recorded as blank or show-through only, with no independent content.
Because it is bleed-through, 'third[?]' can be confirmed from the recto transcription: it reads 'third letter to Bentley'.

Minor orthographic variants ('any thing' vs 'anything', punctuation, opening quotation mark and capital 'That') should follow the recto reading. The machine transcription of the mirrored text is otherwise substantively correct.
